takeaways.headline: No attack slipped through as normal traffic.
takeaways.detail: Across 90 mixed campaigns of four simultaneous attacks, every model flagged at least 99.9% of attack flows as malicious.

takeaways.headline: Floods are named exactly: 5 of 5 volumetric floods identified at 99% or better.
takeaways.detail: Flood traffic has a distinct signature in packet sizes, TCP flags and timing, so the detector can say precisely which flood it is.

takeaways.headline: Scans are recognised as scans, but not always named.
takeaways.detail: Reconnaissance is placed in the right category 96% of the time, but the exact scan type only 34% (best model for each). The six nmap modes send nearly identical traffic — respond to a scan as a scan.

takeaways.headline: When a scan is mistaken for something else, it is almost always Slowloris Scan.
takeaways.detail: With Random Forest, 6 of 6 scan types lose 8%-11% of their flows to Slowloris Scan, a slow denial-of-service attack. Both hold long-lived, near-idle connections, so at flow level they look alike. This single confusion is almost all of the error between categories.

takeaways.headline: SVM and Logistic Regression raise too many false alarms on normal traffic.
takeaways.detail: Share of normal flows flagged as attacks: SVM 59%, Logistic Regression 46%. Random Forest is the quietest at 2%. Only 12 unseen normal flows exist per model set, so treat these rates as indicative.

takeaways.headline: Recommended primary detector: Random Forest.
takeaways.detail: It names well-sampled attacks 58% of the time on average, level with Decision Tree, and raises the fewest false alarms (2% of normal flows). To decide whether traffic is a scan at all, Logistic Regression is stronger (best on 6 of 6 scan types), so it is a useful second opinion.

response.what: Floods the target with packets whose source address is forged to match the target's own address, so the victim ends up replying to itself.
response.categorySummary: Someone is trying to overwhelm a charging station or the management system so it stops responding.
response.impact: Stations lose their OCPP link to the CSMS: heartbeats stop, sessions cannot be authorised or billed, and remote control (start, stop, reset, price updates) fails. Drivers see a station that will not start a charge.

owner: Confirm stations are configured for OCPP offline operation, so they keep charging and queue transactions locally while the CSMS link is down.
Check the station display and local logs: a station that has lost its CSMS link should be visibly flagged to drivers rather than failing silently.
csms: Watch for stations dropping heartbeats together; a burst of simultaneous disconnects points at the network, not at individual stations.
Enforce per-connection and per-source rate limits on the OCPP WebSocket endpoint, ideally at a reverse proxy in front of the CSMS.
Hold off remote resets of affected stations until the flood stops — a reset during an attack just adds reconnect load.
analyst: Drop any inbound packet whose source address equals its destination, and apply anti-spoofing ingress filtering (BCP 38 / unicast reverse-path forwarding).
Identify the source address or addresses and block them at the edge firewall.
Enable upstream DDoS scrubbing or ISP-level filtering if the volume exceeds what the local link can absorb.
Capture a short packet sample for the incident record before blocking, so the attack can be characterised later.

response.what: Probes a range of ports to find which ones are open.
response.categorySummary: Someone is mapping the charging network — finding which devices exist, which ports are open, and what software they run. Nothing is broken yet, but this is usually the step before an attack.
response.impact: No direct outage. The risk is what comes next: an attacker who knows the firmware version and open services can target a known vulnerability in the station or the CSMS.

owner: Make sure station firmware is current — reconnaissance is typically looking for a known, unpatched weakness.
Ask the vendor which ports the station needs; anything beyond OCPP to the CSMS and the local ISO 15118 link to the vehicle should be closed.
csms: Require OCPP security profile 2 or 3 (TLS, with client certificates in profile 3) so a mapped station still cannot be impersonated.
Review recent configuration changes and authorisation attempts from the stations that were scanned.
analyst: Compare the scanned ports against what each station is supposed to expose; any unexpected open port is the finding.
Find the scanning device. In this testbed that was either a host on the station wifi or a compromised vehicle on the charging cable — they call for different containment.
Put charging stations on an isolated network segment that only permits traffic to the CSMS.
Raise monitoring on the scanned hosts: a follow-up exploitation attempt is the thing to catch.

Review recent configuration changes and authorisation attempts from the stations that were scanned.
analyst: Check the versions that were exposed against known vulnerabilities.
Find the scanning device. In this testbed that was either a host on the station wifi or a compromised vehicle on the charging cable — they call for different containment.
Put charging stations on an isolated network segment that only permits traffic to the CSMS.
Raise monitoring on the scanned hosts: a follow-up exploitation attempt is the thing to catch.
